items.title: Houston Person Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995…
items.q: a good album side by Ellington

ctx.x: the people, and that’s elaborate, I’m elaborating, cause I don’t know I’m not a statistician, you know, but most of the people haven’t been to a museum or a play, a ballet, anything. So you get everybody computer literate, and then send them way across the world to Japan, they know nothing about the culture. So then you find us in trouble with our nation, because nobody knows the culture. So I mean now you’ve got a trade war with them, and we don’t even understand their culture. It’s crazy. You take geography…

I was going to ask you that, because you know I’m of the opinion, and I just want to get a thought from you on this. I’m of the opinion that I don’t think if the person who planted that bomb, the same morning he did that, had sat down and listened to a Mozart symphony or a good album side by Ellington, I don’t think he could have put that bomb there.

That’s what I was talking about, getting everybody computer literate with no compassion. Cause there’s no art. I went to a movie, I saw a movie, Martin Sheen was in it, I don’t remember what it was, but it was about he was making a statement about teachers. And one teacher liking Shakespeare and Mozart, and Martin Sheen answers, say, “well I’m not worried about him ‘cause as long as he does that he’ll have compassion.” You know he was talking about the science, of this guy who was in science, but he still…

items.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: who could have more dignity than Duke Ellington?

ctx.x: Yeah, oh man, suave, elegant, and a showman. Even that was a part of the show. And these guys were top musicians, I mean the best. But they never lost sight of that audience.

They brought something, and there was no dignity lost, because who could have more dignity than Duke Ellington? So musicians, you’re always going to have some people that are more serious and that’s good too. I mean there’s a place for — jazz is so big and so wide a range of feelings, you can have everything. Just know what’s what. And there are times when there are concert situations, and there should be times there are dance situations. And I don’t mean swing dancing, I mean with the ballet or Alvin Ailey, they…
I will quote your last interview. You said: “everything in balance.”
